intro: A restless dance is interrupted by a procession heard at a distance. The procession grows until its broad brass line and the quick festive figures occupy the same space; afterwards, the movement withdraws rather than ending in a blaze. The third movement, Sirènes, is not included here because the women’s chorus in this recording has not been fully identified.
question: How does Debussy make two different kinds of motion seem to approach, meet and move apart?

sections.label: A · Festive motion
sections.mNote: quick figures circulate through strings and winds

sections.label: B · The distant procession
sections.mNote: a quiet repeated bass supports muted trumpets

sections.label: B′ · Procession and festival together
sections.mNote: the broad brass line meets the quick festive figures

sections.label: A′ · The dance resumes
sections.mNote: quick woodwind and string motion returns after the massed crest

sections.label: Coda · Receding activity
sections.mNote: fragments and repeated low figures carry the scene away

cues.title: Activity before a long tune
cues.text: Across the opening, quick violin figures and sustained high flute sounds create two different layers. Listen for the short rhythmic cells as they circulate: the energy depends on repetition and changing accents, not on one long melody dominating the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Viewed original score p. 19 and Jobert p. 18 share the flute and violin opening. The report rises rapidly from the low first window to −11 dB at 10–15 s. The performing edition is not established, so added opening reed chords in the revised score are not asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A crest does not finish the dance
cues.text: The early music repeatedly swells and drops back without losing its quick motion. Try following a small rhythmic gesture across those changes in weight: an orchestral retreat need not be the end of the phrase.
cues.evidence: The report reaches a strong 35–40 s window, falls markedly by 45–50 s and continues with frequent attacks through 55–85 s. This supports the changing contour and continued activity, not an instrument-by-instrument account.

cues.title: Not simply music for a night
cues.text: Debussy explained that the title Nocturnes concerned changing impressions of light and colour, rather than the customary piano form. Fêtes turns that idea into a crowd scene: brilliance, movement and distance are compositional materials, not merely a title added afterwards.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s programme statement, reproduced in the LA Philharmonic work note: https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes. The final sentence is an editorial reading of that stated programme.

cues.title: Another surge inside the same scene
cues.text: Through this passage, the festival gathers weight again. Keep the quick underlying motion in mind during the broader swell, so that the following retreat sounds like a change of scale within one scene rather than a completely new beginning.
cues.evidence: Relative level climbs from about −25.5 dB at 85 s to −4.5 dB at 110 s, then drops at 115 s. These within-file windows establish a broad surge; they do not establish a new formal section or a particular written dynamic.

cues.title: A procession enters the picture
cues.text: In Debussy’s own programme, a fantastic procession passes through the festivities and merges with them. That description offers a useful large-scale map: first contrasting motions, then their coexistence, rather than a story requiring named characters or a particular ceremony.
cues.evidence: The LA Philharmonic reproduces Debussy’s description of Fêtes and the procession passing through the festive scene: https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes. No real-world procession is identified in this annotation.

cues.title: Distance made from small sounds
cues.text: In the quieter procession, repeated low notes and soft timpani establish a regular tread; muted trumpets carry the broader line above it. Listen for how the music can seem to approach simply by adding weight to material that is already present.
cues.evidence: Viewed original score p. 43, rehearsal 10, and Jobert pp. 42–43 show the low pulse, two harps, timpani and subsequent muted-trumpet line. The report drops sharply at 156 s, remains quiet through 175 s, then rises progressively. This is a passage estimate, not a trumpet-entry timestamp.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two motions begin to share space
cues.text: As the procession grows, listen for the broad brass line against quicker figures recalling the opening. The point is not to choose one as the real theme: the festival and procession can be superimposed, making an arrival through accumulated layers.
cues.evidence: Original score pp. 47–49 and Jobert pp. 46–48 lead into rehearsal 13, where brass writing meets fast string and wind figures. Relative level rises across 200–245 s, with a change at 220 s. The proposed join is provisional and describes a growing overlap.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lightness after the massed crest
cues.text: After the combined passage, the first tempo returns and quick woodwind movement comes back into focus. Compare this lighter activity with the preceding mass of sound: familiar festive material can resume without repeating the entire opening or rebuilding the procession from scratch.
cues.evidence: Viewed original score p. 53 and Jobert p. 52, rehearsal 14, mark 1er tempo and 6/8 with flowing flute lines, short reed figures and a cello pulse. The report falls from the 240–250 s crest to a much lower 250–260 s level; the boundary is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recorded in 1951, issued in 1952
cues.text: Ansermet and the Orchestre de la Suisse Romande recorded these Nocturnes in Geneva in October 1951. The Decca LP LXT 2637 appeared in March 1952, coupled with Ravel’s Rapsodie espagnole. A session date and a publication date answer different questions.
cues.evidence: Philip Stuart’s Decca discography, p. 24, S080, gives October 1951, Victoria Hall and the March 1952 LXT 2637 issue: https://charm.rhul.ac.uk/pubs/DeccaS.pdf. The exact October day for Nocturnes is not specified; the 10th and 12th belong to other works in the session listing.

cues.title: The scene starts to recede
cues.text: In the closing region, the quick figures survive in smaller, more separated gestures. Listen for the persistence of motion beneath the diminishing weight: the festival is being heard from farther away, not stopped by one decisive final chord.
cues.evidence: Jobert pp. 62–69 and original pp. 63–70 progressively reduce the scoring and retain short rhythmic cells. The report falls steeply after 305–310 s and stays substantially below the earlier crests. The start of the coda is an editorial passage boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Still moving as it disappears
cues.text: At the end, the score leaves a faint snare-drum rhythm and repeated low-string figures after the wind fragments have ebbed away. Notice the difference between motion fading into distance and a ceremonial conclusion: the last page keeps the mechanism moving quietly.
cues.evidence: Viewed original score p. 70 and Jobert p. 69 specify ppp snare and cello/bass figures, with the strings marked as moving ever farther away. Relative level falls through 355–375 s. The note describes the final passage, not an aligned final drum stroke.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The crowd gives way to a tread
transitions.how: The active first span is cut back to a quiet repeated foundation. Debussy marks Modéré mais toujours très rythmé: moderate, but still strongly rhythmic. In 2/4, low strings, harp and timpani establish the new tread before muted trumpets disclose the procession’s broad line. The written accompaniment alternates A♭ and E♭, making a stable bass background rather than continuing the opening’s restless circulation. Distance is created by reduced scoring and level, while pulse remains conspicuous.
transitions.evidence: Viewed original p. 43 and Jobert p. 42, rehearsal 10, supply the heading, 2/4, A♭/E♭ bass and initial scoring. The report’s strongest novelty peak is 156 s; relative level drops from about −7 dB at 150 s to below −33 dB at 155–170 s. This anchors a provisional passage join, not the subsequent trumpet attack.

transitions.title: The procession fills the festive space
transitions.how: The procession does not stop to make room for the festival. Its broad line gains trumpets and low brass while the quicker wind and string figures circulate around it. Timpani, snare and cymbals increase the weight of the arrival, and the brass are asked to sound full-toned without harshness. The join is an accumulation of layers: two kinds of motion become simultaneous over the continuing rhythmic foundation, rather than being separated by a cadence or silence.
transitions.evidence: Original p. 48 and Jobert p. 47, rehearsal 13, show the broad brass line, rapid strings, wind cells and percussion together. The report rises steadily across 200–245 s with a novelty peak at 220 s; the maximum five-second window is 245 s. The span is estimated rather than rehearsal-number aligned.

transitions.title: The mass dissolves into quick figures
transitions.how: After the massed passage, 1er tempo restores the quicker movement. The score changes to 6/8 and pares back the brass and percussion, leaving flowing flute lines, short reed figures and an articulated cello foundation. The return recovers the festival’s kind of motion, rather than presenting the opening orchestration unchanged. Its lightness is especially apparent against the procession’s broad, heavily supported line.
transitions.evidence: Viewed original p. 53 and Jobert p. 52, rehearsal 14: 1er tempo, 6/8, winds and cello figure after the massed crest. The report falls from −4 dB at 245 s to about −21 dB at 250–260 s. The join uses this conspicuous change as a provisional anchor; no bar-alignment claim is made.

transitions.title: The festivities leave fragments behind
transitions.how: The late festive surge is not sealed by a grand final cadence. Debussy reduces the texture to short wind recollections and repeating string figures; later, soft brass and the procession’s distant character are remembered. The closing pages further loosen the metre and ask for restraint before leaving low strings and snare drum in motion. The ending therefore transforms both earlier scenes by subtraction: gestures remain recognisable as their orchestral surroundings disappear.
transitions.evidence: Jobert pp. 62–69; original pp. 69–70 were also viewed for the last mixed-metre fragments and the withdrawing low-string/snare ending. The report changes at 312 s after a final 305–310 s surge, with smaller peaks and a very quiet final tail. The coda start is a broad editorial division, not a precise written tempo change.

source.title: Debussy, Nocturnes, original orchestral score, Kalmus reprint of Fromont
source.locator: Fêtes, printed pp. 19–70; opening, rehearsals 10, 13, 14 and closing pages viewed. Cross-checked with Jobert 1930 pp. 18–69, Sibley http://hdl.handle.net/1802/30697. Timings are provisional passage estimates, not instrument detection or a verified performing edition. Harp groups both harps; percussion groups snare drum and cymbals. Groups can play intermittently within a highlighted passage.

timeline.note: Provisional opening map: fast violin cells under sustained flutes, common to both viewed editions. Revised-edition added reed chords are not asserted for this recording.
Provisional early span: reed figures and short brass punctuation join the circulating string rhythm; this is not a simultaneous-entry map.
Provisional opening continuation: upper-wind figures are set against continuing string activity and held horn colours.
Provisional approach to the procession: winds and strings exchange short figures while timpani and lower voices articulate the foundation.
Provisional rehearsal-10 opening: very quiet harp, timpani and low-string tread; the trumpets have not yet stated the procession line.
Provisional procession span: muted trumpets carry the broad phrase above the repeated low foundation; their first attack is not time-aligned.
Provisional approach: wind replies, horn activity and increasingly active strings enlarge the procession.
Provisional combined passage: broad brass and fast string material coexist, with wind interjections, both harps and percussion. Not every group plays continuously.
Provisional rehearsal-14 region: flowing woodwinds and the cello pulse emerge after the massed arrival; upper strings rejoin within the passage.
Provisional late festival: high winds and string motion regain weight, with horns and rhythmic support.
Provisional receding region: short wind and soft brass recollections pass over persistent low-string cells; the map groups intermittent gestures.
Provisional last fragments: exposed wind turns, soft low-brass support and plucked string chords replace the earlier orchestral mass.
Provisional last-page estimate: snare drum and low strings continue quietly into the distance; no exact final attack or release is claimed.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
